なに を しますか — What do you do?
You say what you eat, drink, read, listen to and watch: the direct object with を, the place of an action with で, and suggestions with ～ましょう.
I bought a shirt at the shop.
To use を for what you eat, drink, read, watch (the direct object).
To ask なに を しますか (what do you do?) and answer.
To say where you do an action with で.
To suggest something: ～ましょう (let’s…) and ～ませんか (won’t you…?).
To say how often: いつも, よく, ときどき, あまり + negative.
Yuki’s mother, Mrs Tanaka, has arrived in Madrid. On Sunday, at Kenji’s café, she meets Mihai and Ana.
Mum, this is Mihai and this is Ana.
Nice to meet you. I’m Mihai. Pleased to meet you.
I’m Tanaka. Thank you for always looking after Yuki.
These are oranges from Valencia. Please, have them.
Oh, thank you! Oranges are expensive in Japan.
Well then, what will you have to drink?
I’ll have a coffee. And you, Ana?
An orange juice for me! Hee-hee.
Mihai, what do you do on your days off?
I often read books. Sometimes I watch films.
Mihai is always studying Japanese at the library.
I play tennis in the park. And I listen to music.
I see. I don’t watch much television. But I write letters every day.
Everyone: today’s lunch is fish. Won’t you eat with us?
“osewa ni natte imasu” = thank you for looking after (set phrase)
The character を only appears as a particle and is read “o”, just like お. なに を = “nani o”.
Careful: ききます (I listen) has two “ki”s, きます (I come) only one. The first i in “kiki” almost disappears: “k’kimas”.
A small ゃ joins the syllable before it: ちゃ = “cha” (one syllable), not “chi-ya”.
The particle を (read “o”) goes AFTER the thing the action is done to: WHAT you eat, WHAT you drink, WHAT you read.
The order is always: WHAT を + VERB. In English “I eat bread”, in Japanese “bread-o eat”. The verb comes LAST.
The question: なに を ～ます か (what…?). なに を たべます か = What do you eat?
します = to do. It combines with lots of nouns to make new verbs:
なにも (nothing) ONLY goes with a negative verb: なにも しません. Like どこ へ も いきません in chapter 5.
3. Where you do the action: で
Review from chapters 3–4: に = where you ARE / where you GO; で = where you DO something.
I play tennis in the park.
The full sentence: WHO は — WHEN — WHERE で — WHAT を — VERB. わたし は まいにち うち で ごはん を たべます.
4. Suggestions: ～ましょう and ～ませんか
To suggest something, change ～ます into:
That’s how it’s done in Japan: one person invites with ～ませんか, the other accepts with ～ましょう. That’s exactly what happened at the end of the dialogue.
The typical mistake: “あまり みます”. あまり and ぜんぜん must take a negative verb!
A polite invitation: “Won’t you have some tea?”
I bought fish at the market.
What does Mrs Tanaka do every day?
おかあさん の てがみ — Mum’s letter
Mrs Tanaka writes a letter, as she does every day. This time, to her sister in Kyoto.
To Michiko. How are you? I’m in Madrid now.
Every morning I eat bread with Yuki and drink coffee.
Spaniards don’t drink much tea. It’s a little sad.
Yesterday I had lunch with Yuki’s friends.
Mihai is a doctor. He’s a very serious person.
Ana is a lively person. She’s always laughing.
In the afternoon I bought Yuki a jumper at the department store.
Next week I’m going back to Japan. I’ll buy lots of souvenirs, OK?
What do Mum and Yuki drink in the morning?
Why is Mrs Tanaka a little sad?
さいご の ひ — The last day
Today is Mum’s last day in Madrid.
Tomorrow morning she flies back to Japan.
Last night, Yuki wrote a plan in a notebook.
Eight o’clock. The two of them had breakfast at home.
Today there’s no bread. Yuki made rice and miso soup.
“Oh, a Japanese breakfast! Thank you.” Mum was very happy.
Ten o’clock. The two of them went to the Prado museum.
At the museum they saw lots of old paintings.
Mum likes Goya’s paintings. “This painting is a bit scary, isn’t it?”
Photos aren’t allowed. So Mum drew in her notebook.
One o’clock. They had lunch at Kenji’s place.
Kenji had prepared a special set menu.
Spanish fish and Japanese soy sauce. “Delicious! Is it Spanish or Japanese?”
Three o’clock. The two of them bought souvenirs at the department store.
For Dad they bought wine. For Aunt Michiko, a scarf.
Then they ate churros at a café and drank hot chocolate.
Seven o’clock. Mihai and Ana came to Yuki’s place too.
They all had dinner together and listened to Romanian and Japanese songs.
“What’s this?” “It’s cozonac. A kind of Romanian cake.”
Eleven at night. Mum opened her notebook and showed it to Yuki.
In it were the Goya painting, Kenji’s menu and everyone’s faces.
“Yuki, you have good friends. I can stop worrying.”
Yuki didn’t say anything. But she cried a little.
Why did Mum draw at the museum?
What did Mihai bring in the evening?
Won’t you have some tea with me?
Kenji has written the menu of the day on the board. Read it.
Today’s lunch is the fish set.
It also comes with rice, miso soup and vegetables.
You don’t eat meat? No problem. We also have a vegetable set.
The drink is tea. The tea is free!
For dessert, please have some oranges.
Someone doesn’t eat meat. What can they order?
